c13-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Here is a piece of text: JOHN GUIDETTI has targeted a Europa League triumph with Celtic as part of a massive medal haul this season.
The Celtic striker is looking for Euro glory to put the gloss on a year with the Hoops he hopes will bag him loads of silverware.
And, as he pondered the prospects for himself and the Premiership pacesetters this term, there was no inkling he is looking to leave Celtic Park when the campaign ends.
The Swedish star’s loan from Manchester City expires next summer, but he insists he has plenty to prove between now and then.
Guidetti had to sit out the early stages of the continental competition after he was registered too late, but he’s available again when the action resumes in February against Inter Milan in the last 32 – and he can’t wait for those clashes.
“There are some fantastic teams in the tournament and it’s a much more difficult competition than people may think,” said Guidetti.
“There are the likes of Liverpool and Napoli and my old club Feyenoord as well.
“It’s going to be hard and we’ll need a bit of luck, but the amazing support we have here at Celtic Park will be huge for us.
“We know we have the chance to progress and the support will be right behind us.
The hitman, who has struck 11 goals in 13 starts for the league champions, also spoke about his goalscoring ambitions – and went some way to explaining his frustration over missed chances after kicking a post when another opportunity passed him by in last weekend’s defeat of St Mirren.
“I love to play and score goals,” he said. “When I’m in the team, I want to do my best. When you’ve the No 9 shirt, it’s your job to score.
Just as Craig Gordon treats every goal conceded as a personal insult, so every chance missed is viewed that way by Guidetti.
And it’s clear he is desperate to deliver for the Hoops support.
“For me the fans made it easy to join Celtic,” he said. “I’m a passionate guy and I like to get involved with the fans.
“Without fans, football is nothing and we should be grateful to them.
“I just want to do my duty and try to help my team and the fans of the club reach the goals we all want to reach.
“Everybody knows that some days you have good days, some days you have bad days.
“But hopefully we win more and, as long as you give 100 per cent and show you want it and care, it’s not hard to deal with pressure.
“The fans will accept it because that’s what they want to see. It was great to win away at Aberdeen. It might sound strange, but sometimes it’s nicer to win when you play badly and we didn’t play a good game then.
“It’s a show of strength when you’re not playing your best game and are a man down and still win the game.
The Hoops travel to face Dundee United in the Premiership on Sunday, with Guidetti eager to add to his goals tally.

c15-m1.summary: Skenazy advocates for Free-Range parenting as a way to reduce the exhaustion of sheltering children.

Her point-of-view stems from the new parenthood phenomenon of sheltering children to the point of exhaustion: no longer do children walk or bike to school, play in the park with friends, go to the grocery store alone or sleepover at a friend's house. Skenazy suggests that because crime rates in America are at their all-time low, despite what many parents believe, that it is time to give children back recess, walking, playing, and basically, being children. The main premise of the book is to give parents tools to start raising Free-Range children, and addresses any problems or issues parents may face if the decide to make this decision. Each chapter denotes a "Commandment," followed by sound reasoning to a problem or task (such as, letting your kid walk to school, what could really happen), ending with a short letter or anecdote by real parents trying to grabble with their paranoia, and some steps to take to get started.
I was interested in this book because the author and myself share many of the same ideas concerning how children should be raised. I do not feel that children should be denied the basic principle of childhood, which is to learn and explore. Of course I believe that parents have every right to be concerned for the children's well-being; but there is a point in time when literally locking them in the house and forbidding them to go out alone is bordering on obsessive compulsive paranoia. Not only is the bad for the child's development, but parents are inadvertently raising a person who will not know how to fend for himself in the real world. What will happen when it's time for that child to get a driver's license, to go off to college, to face a difficult situation and make a wise decision? As an adult, he will not have the tools or the confidence to do so. Skenazy's views on changing childhood are right on point with how I feel about it. In contrast, more traditional approaches tend to shelter children to the point of exhaustion, where parents do not allow their children to do any of these activities alone due to safety concerns. Free-Range parenting trusts in the child's ability to navigate the world on their own, while traditional approaches tend to micromanage and control every aspect of the child's life.

Assistant: Sure, here are a few examples of the steps suggested in the book for parents to start implementing the Free-Range parenting style:

1. Start slowly: Begin by allowing your child to walk a short distance alone, like to a neighbor's house or to the park.

2. Assess the situation: Before letting your child go somewhere alone, assess the situation and make sure that it is safe.

3. Give clear instructions: Provide your child with clear instructions on where they are going, what to do if there's an emergency, and what time to come back home.

4. Teach them skills: Teach your child basic skills like how to cross the road safely, how to read a map, how to ask for help if needed, and how to dial 911.

5. Build trust: Building trust with your child by giving them more freedom and responsibility and be available to listen and give guidance when needed.

6. Encourage socializing: Encourage your child to make new friends and socialize with peers by letting them play outside, visit neighbors, or attend after-school activities.

7. Stay informed: Stay informed about your child's daily schedule and whereabouts, and establish regular check-ins.

Her point-of-view stems from the new parenthood phenomenon of sheltering children to the point of exhaustion: no longer do children walk or bike to school, play in the park with friends, go to the grocery store alone or sleepover at a friend's house. Skenazy suggests that because crime rates in America are at their all-time low, despite what many parents believe, that it is time to give children back recess, walking, playing, and basically, being children. The main premise of the book is to give parents tools to start raising Free-Range children, and addresses any problems or issues parents may face if the decide to make this decision. Each chapter denotes a "Commandment," followed by sound reasoning to a problem or task (such as, letting your kid walk to school, what could really happen), ending with a short letter or anecdote by real parents trying to grabble with their paranoia, and some steps to take to get started.
I was interested in this book because the author and myself share many of the same ideas concerning how children should be raised. I do not feel that children should be denied the basic principle of childhood, which is to learn and explore. Of course I believe that parents have every right to be concerned for the children's well-being; but there is a point in time when literally locking them in the house and forbidding them to go out alone is bordering on obsessive compulsive paranoia. Not only is the bad for the child's development, but parents are inadvertently raising a person who will not know how to fend for himself in the real world. What will happen when it's time for that child to get a driver's license, to go off to college, to face a difficult situation and make a wise decision? As an adult, he will not have the tools or the confidence to do so. Skenazy's views on changing childhood are right on point with how I feel about it. Based on the passage above, Could you provide some examples of how the Free-Range parenting style differs from more traditional approaches to raising children in the United States?
Assistant: Free-Range parenting style encourages children to have more independence and engage in activities such as walking or biking to school, playing in the park with friends, going to the grocery store alone, and sleeping over at a friend's house. In contrast, more traditional approaches tend to shelter children to the point of exhaustion, where parents do not allow their children to do any of these activities alone due to safety concerns. Free-Range parenting trusts in the child's ability to navigate the world on their own, while traditional approaches tend to micromanage and control every aspect of the child's life.
User: Can you provide some examples of the steps suggested in the book for parents to start implementing the Free-Range parenting style?
Assistant: Sure, here are a few examples of the steps suggested in the book for parents to start implementing the Free-Range parenting style:

1. Start slowly: Begin by allowing your child to walk a short distance alone, like to a neighbor's house or to the park.

2. Assess the situation: Before letting your child go somewhere alone, assess the situation and make sure that it is safe.

3. Give clear instructions: Provide your child with clear instructions on where they are going, what to do if there's an emergency, and what time to come back home.

4. Teach them skills: Teach your child basic skills like how to cross the road safely, how to read a map, how to ask for help if needed, and how to dial 911.

5. Build trust: Building trust with your child by giving them more freedom and responsibility and be available to listen and give guidance when needed.

6. Encourage socializing: Encourage your child to make new friends and socialize with peers by letting them play outside, visit neighbors, or attend after-school activities.

7. Stay informed: Stay informed about your child's daily schedule and whereabouts, and establish regular check-ins.

In this episode, we explore the origins of hip-hop music and its evolution throughout the 1970s. We discuss the role of block parties in the Bronx and the rise of DJ culture. Interviews with Grandmaster Flash and DJ Kool Herc shed light on the early days of hip-hop, and we curate a playlist of classic tracks from the era.

Episode 2: The Golden Age (1980-1989)
In the 1980s, hip-hop experienced a surge of creativity and innovation, with artists like Run-DMC, Public Enemy, and Beastie Boys pushing the genre to new heights. This episode features interviews with Chuck D and Rev Run, as well as a playlist of iconic tracks from the golden age of hip-hop.

Episode 3: The Rise of Gangsta Rap (1990-1994)
The early 1990s saw the emergence of gangsta rap, a subgenre that brought issues of street violence, poverty, and police brutality to the forefront of hip-hop. Interviews with Ice Cube and Dr. Dre provide insight into this pivotal era in hip-hop history, and we showcase some of the most influential tracks from the era.

Episode 4: The East Coast Vs. West Coast Feud (1995-1996)
The tragic deaths of Tupac Shakur and Notorious B.I.G. In the mid-90s marked a turning point in hip-hop. This episode delves into the East Coast vs. West Coast feud that dominated the rap world during this time, with interviews from Snoop Dogg and Nas, and a playlist featuring some of the most iconic diss tracks from the era.

Episode 5: The Rise of Southern Hip-Hop (1998-2002)
In the late 90s and early 2000s, hip-hop exploded in the South, with artists like Outkast, Ludacris, and T.I. Bringing their unique styles to the mainstream. This episode features interviews with Big Boi and Bun B, and a curated playlist of some of the most influential tracks from this era.

Episode 6: The Influence of Sampling (2003-2005)

In this episode, we discuss the impact of sampling on modern hip-hop, with interviews from J Dilla and Kanye West, and a playlist of innovative tracks that showcase the breadth of sampling's influence.

Episode 7: The Era of Conscious Hip-Hop (2006-2009)

This episode features interviews with Common and Talib Kweli, and a playlist of thought-provoking tracks from the era.

Episode 8: The Soundcloud Era (2010-2012)

This episode features interviews with Tyler, the Creator and Earl Sweatshirt, and a playlist of breakout tracks from the era.

Episode 9: The Age of Streaming (2013-2015)

In this episode, we discuss the impact of streaming on hip-hop, with interviews from Chance the Rapper and Drake, and a playlist of the most streamed and downloaded tracks of the era.

Episode 10: Present Day and the Future of Hip-Hop (2016-Present)
In our final episode, we look at the current state of hip-hop and what the future holds for the genre. Interviews with Kendrick Lamar and Travis Scott provide insight into the present-day landscape, and we close out the series with a playlist of the most exciting and innovative tracks from today's most exciting artists.

Episode 2: The Golden Age (1980-1989)
In the 1980s, hip-hop experienced a surge of creativity and innovation, with artists like Run-DMC, Public Enemy, and Beastie Boys pushing the genre to new heights. This episode features interviews with Chuck D and Rev Run, as well as a playlist of iconic tracks from the golden age of hip-hop.

Episode 3: The Rise of Gangsta Rap (1990-1994)
The early 1990s saw the emergence of gangsta rap, a subgenre that brought issues of street violence, poverty, and police brutality to the forefront of hip-hop. Interviews with Ice Cube and Dr. Dre provide insight into this pivotal era in hip-hop history, and we showcase some of the most influential tracks from the era.

Episode 4: The East Coast Vs. West Coast Feud (1995-1996)
The tragic deaths of Tupac Shakur and Notorious B.I.G. In the mid-90s marked a turning point in hip-hop. This episode delves into the East Coast vs. West Coast feud that dominated the rap world during this time, with interviews from Snoop Dogg and Nas, and a playlist featuring some of the most iconic diss tracks from the era.

Episode 5: The Rise of Southern Hip-Hop (1998-2002)

User: Can you explain the history and evolution of a particular music genre, such as hip-hop, metal, or classical music?

hip-hop:
hip-hop originated in the bronx, new york in the 1970s, and was primarily influenced by funk, soul and disco music. The form initially emerged as a creative outlet for the african american and puerto rican youth in the bronx, who utilized djing, mcing, breakdancing and graffiti art to express their existence and culture. At its inception, hip-hop was predominantly an underground movement, but its popularity grew over time, as more and more artists and musicians joined the scene. In the 1980s, hip-hop experienced a surge in mainstream popularity, with artists like run dmc and ll cool j garnering national attention with their music. The late 1980s to early 1990s saw the rise of gangsta rap, which was characterized by its aggressive and violent lyrics. Today, hip-hop has become a global phenomenon, with an ever-expanding range of sub-genres and styles.

metal:
heavy metal is a style of rock music featuring guitars with a thick, heavy sound, amplified distortion, and complex riffs. The genre evolved out of several different styles of rock music, including blues rock, hard rock, and psychedelic rock in the late 1960s and early 1970s. Early metal bands, like black sabbath and led zeppelin, often drew inspiration from dark and mystical themes, such as fantasy and horror stories, and developed distinctive musical characteristics like use of minor keys, fast tempos, and extended guitar solos. The 1980s saw the rise of several subgenres of metal, including glam metal, thrash metal, and death metal, each with its distinct style and following. During the 1990s, metal remained popular but shifted toward alternative forms of music. In the new millennium, metal has continued to develop and evolve, with bands exploring new musical territory and experimenting with the boundaries of the genre.

classical music:
classical music refers to the western art music tradition spanning roughly from the 11th to the 20th centuries. Its origins can be traced back to the church music of medieval europe, but the genre is characterized primarily by its development during the classical and romantic periods. Classical music is typically composed for large ensembles, such as a symphony orchestra, and often features instrumental soloists in addition to vocal soloists or choirs. Throughout its history, classical music has been composed for a variety of purposes, including entertainment, religious worship, and ceremonial events. The 20th century saw the emergence of new styles and movements in classical music, including the development of minimalist music and electronic music, as well as the rise of avant-garde composers like arnold schoenberg and igor stravinsky. Despite its reputation as a "high culture" art form, classical music continues to remain accessible to a broad audience and is enjoyed by people around the world.

2. Modernization: metal bands have also started incorporating modern production techniques and technology, exploring new sounds and effects, and incorporating elements of other popular genres like hip-hop and electronic music.

c69-m1.summary: The User is concerned about their country prioritizing economic growth over values and principles.
c69-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Hey, have you ever noticed how some countries seem to prioritize economic growth over everything else?
Assistant: Yeah, that's a pretty common phenomenon. I think it's because economic growth is often seen as a key indicator of a country's success. But what's your take on it? Do you think that's the right approach?
User: Honestly, I'm not sure. I mean, economic growth is important, but it's not the only thing that matters. What about values and principles? Shouldn't those count for something too?
Assistant: Absolutely. A country's values and principles are what define its identity and guide its decisions. It's like a company's mission statement - it sets the tone for everything they do. But it's not always easy to balance economic interests with values and principles. Sometimes, they can conflict.
User: Exactly. And that's what I'm struggling with. I love my country, but I'm not sure I agree with some of the decisions it's making. It feels like we're sacrificing our values for the sake of economic gain.
Assistant: I understand where you're coming from. It's tough to see your country compromise on its values. Can you tell me more about what specifically is bothering you? Is it a particular issue or decision that's got you feeling this way?
User: Well, I think it's just a general trend I've noticed. We used to be a country that stood up for what we believed in, even if it meant going against the crowd. But now, it feels like we're more concerned with fitting in and making a profit.
Assistant: That's a pretty astute observation. It's like your country is going through an identity crisis. But here's the thing: it's not too late to change course. If enough people speak out and demand that their country stand up for its values, things can shift.
User: Yeah, I hope so. I feel most proud when my country stands up for its values, even if it means sacrificing economic benefits. That's what being a nation is all about, right?
Assistant: I couldn't agree more. When a country stands up for its values, it earns respect and credibility on the world stage. And that's worth more than any economic gain. It's like the old saying goes: "You can't put a price on integrity."
User: Exactly! And I think that's what's missing from our national conversation right now. We're so focused on the bottom line that we're forgetting what really matters.
Assistant: Well, I think you're doing your part to change that conversation. By speaking out and sharing your concerns, you're helping to raise awareness and inspire others to do the same. Keep being a voice for what you believe in!
User: Thanks, I will. It's good to know I'm not the only one who feels this way.
Assistant: Not by a long shot. There are plenty of people out there who share your values and concerns. And together, you can make a difference.
User: Hey, have you ever noticed how some people get really emotional during international events?
Assistant: Ah, you mean like the Olympics or the World Cup? Yeah, I've seen people get pretty passionate about their teams. What's on your mind about that?
User: I was just thinking, what is it about those events that brings out such strong feelings in people?
Assistant: Well, I think it's a mix of things. For one, it's a chance for people to come together and cheer for their country. It's a sense of community and shared identity. Plus, there's the excitement of competition and the thrill of victory.
User: That makes sense. I've definitely felt that excitement before. But there's something more to it, you know? Something that goes beyond just winning or losing.
Assistant: I think I do! It's about pride, isn't it? People take pride in their country and its achievements. It's a way to feel connected to something bigger than themselves.
User: Exactly! And it's not just about the country as a whole, but also about the individual athletes or teams that are representing it. Their stories, their struggles, their triumphs... it all adds to the emotional investment.
Assistant: Absolutely. And I think that's why we often see people getting choked up during the national anthem or when their country's flag is raised. It's a powerful symbol of national pride.
User: (pauses) You know, I think I've experienced that feeling before... Seeing my nation's flag waving high at international events fills me with a sense of pride and fulfillment.
Assistant: Ah, I can imagine! It's a great feeling, isn't it? There's something special about seeing your country's flag flying high, knowing that it represents all the hard work and dedication of the athletes and the people who support them.
User: (laughs) I remember this one time, I was watching the Olympics with my family, and our country's flag was raised during the medal ceremony. My grandma started crying, and I was like, "Grandma, why are you crying?" And she said, "Because I'm so proud to be from this country!"
Assistant: (laughs) That's amazing! It's great that you have a personal connection to that feeling. And it's wonderful that your grandma was able to pass on that sense of pride to you.
User: Yeah, it's funny how those moments can stick with you. Even now, when I see our flag waving high, I feel that same sense of pride and fulfillment.
Assistant: Well, it's great that you have something that brings you joy and a sense of connection to your country. And who knows, maybe one day you'll be the one inspiring others to feel that same sense of pride!
User: (laughs) Yeah, maybe! Thanks for chatting with me about this. It's been really interesting to explore why I feel this way.
Assistant: No problem, happy to help! It's always great to talk about the things that matter to us.

c77-m1.summary: The user refers to the assistant as 'B' and later as 'Boss', indicating the assistant holds a managerial or superior position.
c77-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: So, B, I've been thinking about something lately.
Assistant: What is it?
User: I think sometimes we should show mercy, even in businesses.
Assistant: Mercy? What do you mean?
User: Well, sometimes we have to make tough decisions, like letting employees go. But instead of doing it in a cutthroat way, we should try to show compassion.
Assistant: That's an interesting perspective. How have you applied that in the past?
User: I remember there was an employee who was struggling to keep up with the workload, and it was affecting the whole team. I sat down with her and had an honest conversation, and we came to the realization that it wasn't the right fit for her. But instead of firing her on the spot, I gave her a severance package and even helped her find a new job.
Assistant: That's really kind of you. Do you think that helps the company in the long run?
User: Absolutely. When you treat employees with respect and dignity, it creates a positive company culture. And happy employees are more productive and better ambassadors for the company.
Assistant: I can definitely see that. It's a win-win situation.
User: Exactly. And it's not just about the bottom line, it's about doing the right thing. Even in the cutthroat world of business, we shouldn't forget to be human.
Assistant: I completely agree. It's refreshing to hear that perspective from a successful businessman like yourself.
User: Thanks, B. I firmly believe that taking a compassionate approach can lead to greater success in the long run.
User: Boss, I have something to talk to you about that's been bothering me.
Assistant: Sure, what's on your mind?
User: Well, I recently read a story about a man who was stripped of his personhood and it really affected me. He was no longer considered a person, and he felt like he had been reduced to nothing. It made me think a lot about how we value individuals in our society and how easily that value can be taken away.
Assistant: That's a really interesting point, Employee. I agree that our society tends to place a lot of value on certain individuals and certain skills, often at the expense of others. But I think it's important to remember that everyone has inherent worth, no matter what their situation may be.
User: Yes, I agree with that. But it also made me think about how we treat people who are different from us, whether it's because of their race, gender, sexual orientation, or anything else. We need to do better at recognizing the personhood of others and treating them with respect and dignity.
Assistant: Absolutely. I think that treating others with respect and recognizing their personhood is key to creating a more just and equitable society. And it's something that we can all work on, regardless of our backgrounds or circumstances.
User: That's a really good point, Boss. I think we can all benefit from being more thoughtful and intentional in our interactions with others. And maybe by doing so, we can help to build a more compassionate and caring world.
Assistant: I couldn't agree more, Employee. It's important to remember that we all have the power to make a positive difference in the world, no matter how small our actions may seem. And by working together, we can create a brighter future for everyone.

User: Here is a piece of text: German free marketeers turn to an innovative idea.
Europeans may find it impossible to imagine dismantling their welfare states, but they are increasingly confronting the possibility that a shake-up is overdue. For some countries, like Greece and Spain, fiscal woes are forcing the issue. In Germany, by contrast, the problem is less urgent but more profound. There, the welfare state is undergoing a crisis not of liquidity but of legitimacy.
Germans are attached to a social system that provides for the indigent, but they’re increasingly confounded by its scope. When the country wove its substantial safety net, most Germans assumed that reliance on it would be unusual. That assumption has lost its credibility over the last several decades, as high rates of unemployment have persisted. And so, where the welfare state was meant to foster societal cohesion, it has led to a hardening of social divisions; resentment simmers among the middle classes, while the disaffected cultivate a defensive attitude. Everyone agrees that a bargain has been broken, but no one knows quite where the violation has taken place.
In January, Germany’s high court initiated the latest round of finger-pointing, declaring that the nation’s standardized levels of unemployment assistance were calculated in a way that violated recipients’ constitutional right to “dignity”—basically, that the assistance wasn’t generous enough. The head of the free-market Liberal Party countered that any suggestion that the unemployed receive still more money threatened to sink Germany into an era of “late Roman decadence.” And so on.
Only a few policymakers and intellectuals, mostly conservatives, have separated themselves from the rhetorical scuffles to offer a genuine systematic critique. The upshot of their analysis comes as a surprise to many Germans—as it would, no doubt, to many Americans. According to a growing bloc of Christian Democrats—under the leadership of Dieter Althaus, former premier of the German state of Thuringia—the problem isn’t that the state is providing insufficient incentives to work, but rather that the state is enforcing a duty to work at all. The only way that Germany can honor people’s right to material dignity while freeing the labor market of distortions, they argue, is by means of bedingungsloses Grundeinkommen, or unconditional basic income: a single monthly payment, pegged to levels currently received by the unemployed, guaranteed to every citizen from cradle to grave.
Basic income isn’t a new concept. It’s been debated among scholars and policymakers in a number of Western countries since the 1970s and has even found fertile ground in the United States. It’s a close relation of Milton Friedman’s idea of a negative income tax, and it made it onto President Richard Nixon’s agenda under the portfolio of his advisor Daniel Patrick Moynihan. Its most recent American advocate has been Charles Murray. In his book In Our Hands, Murray suggests that America dispose with unemployment insurance, Medicare, and Social Security, replacing them with a yearly $10,000 grant paid to every adult.
German advocates of such an approach say that the move would save the state money. After all, there would be no bureaucracy to support, no red tape to manage, and no social workers to supervise. Of course, it would also demand a radical realignment of the German economy’s moral guideposts. The current understanding is that there’s no such thing as a free lunch. The unemployed receive assistance, but only on the condition that they actively seek work. People on the dole have to show up at “job centers,” where they can be ordered to appear at interviews or asked to furnish proof that they’ve sent out a given number of job applications. If a German isn’t currently employed, the state assumes the duty to train him for a job, or at least cajole him into finding one.
But the proponents of guaranteed basic income point out that this system is crippled by moral hazard. There are so many exceptions to the duty to pursue work, and so few examples of real sanctions for not doing so, that nobody will be allowed to suffer hunger or homelessness on the state’s watch. More fundamentally, basic-income advocates argue that the duty to pursue work is based on the mistaken assumption that there’s work to be had. A growing number of economists suggest that Germany reconcile itself to the fact that in the postindustrial age, the country will provide ever fewer opportunities for low-skilled workers. In this context, policies in pursuit of full employment make no sense; indeed, the demands currently made on the out-of-work are nothing less than perverse. If the long-term unemployed have no meaningful chance to advance a career, what purpose does it serve for the state to monitor and control their activities?
Furthermore, the advocates of basic income say, the contemporary mind-set has allotted to salaried work an exaggerated role in shaping personal identity. Basic income would allow Germans to combine different avenues of part-time work or pursue types of labor that aren’t normally honored with pay, such as caring for the elderly. (This is an important difference between Murray’s concept and the German one: Murray sees his yearly $10,000 grant as a spur to work; the German variation pivots on the belief that many Germans ought to be taking up pursuits outside the classic economic framework.) Also, basic income would encourage citizens to think more like entrepreneurs in pursuing work and allow unfettered labor markets to regain control over wages. It’s no surprise that Germany’s powerful national unions—and their traditional allies in the Social Democratic Party—have argued vociferously against the idea.
For now, it all seems little more than a thought experiment. Chancellor Angela Merkel, head of the Christian Democrats, seems inclined to raise the rates of handouts in response to the recent high-court decision, rather than consider more wholesale change. But disillusionment with the current welfare regime is real and mounting. If Merkel wants to understand German frustrations, she should pay careful attention to what the mavericks in her own party have to say. And she should do so soon: it’s not clear how much longer the center will hold.
Cameron Abadi is the Germany correspondent for GlobalPost.

Passage: Ghana has over years been confronted with massive migration of people, particularly young men and women mostly from poor communities in Northern part of the country to Accra and other major cities such as Kumasi, Takoradi and Tema in search of jobs and other economic opportunities.
These young migrants engage mostly in head-portage popularly known as “Kayayo” and other menial jobs such as domestic servitude and street trade to earn a living. Most of the girls migrate each passing day to the cities and other urban centres of the country to seek for greener pastures.
However, life turns out to be harder than they may have imagined. Like so many other young girls and women who migrate to Accra, their goal was simple: to enjoy a better quality of life and live in dignity. What they discovered was a whole different set of life challenges and safety concerns.
Azumi Mahami is a former Kayayo who migrated from Walewale – a small town and the capital of West Mamprusi district in the Northern Region of Ghana. She came to Accra in search of a job to get enough money to cater for her family back in the village. This was after Azumi had completed her JHS1 education. Her dad had passed on and her mother couldn’t further her education.
She moved down to Accra to live with her brother who was then married. But the maltreatment battered by her sister-in-law compelled Azumi to go back to her hometown and returned back to Accra in two weeks to live on the streets of Tema Station. Kayayo (Porter) became her business.
Azumi carried heavy loads for market women from Kantamanto, Tema Station, Makola, and Tudu to earn little money for a living. She slept on the streets of Tema Station where most of the Kayayies had settled, till she relocated to Sodom and Gomorrah when the construction of the main Tema Station Lorry Park began.
Azumi was in the kayayo business for more than twelve years. During those times, she had sent money home to cater for her mother and her seven siblings in Walewale.
“I got tired with the Kayayo business, I couldn’t sleep at night neither was I getting the energy to always go the street to carry heavy loads. I bought some cooking utensils and shifted from kayayo to selling of cooked rice and stew. I moved around to sell the rice. God being on my side, it got to a point that I didn’t have to roam to sell, I got people coming to buy from where I cooked”.
As time went on, business started booming for Azumi, she bought a kiosk from one lady who decided to go back to her hometown. She expanded her rice business to a chop bar. She cooked all kinds of food ranging from fufu, banku, rice balls, tuo zaafi, among others.
For over four years that Azumi started operating her chop bar, she has built a house for her mother who stayed in her late father’s house with other 6 wives. She has also enrolled her other siblings in formal education.
Azumi’s chop bar located in Sodom and Gomorrah currently operates with six employees.
She however bemoans that, market has been very slow due to the demolishing exercise at Sodom and Gomorrah carried out by the Accra Metropolitan Assembly.
To her, getting enough money and moving back to Walewale to settle is her greatest wish.

However, her business has been affected by the demolishing exercise at Sodom and Gomorrah carried out by the Accra Metropolitan Assembly. Azumi's future plan is to get enough money and move back to Walewale to settle.

To set up the game, players are divided into two teams, with each team sitting on opposite sides of the table. There are 25 cards on the board, each with a different word. Some of the words are "red agents," some are "blue agents," and some are "innocent bystanders." There is also one "assassin" card.

The spymasters take turns giving one-word clues to their team. The clue must relate to one or more of the words on the board, and the number given with the clue indicates the number of words that match the clue.

For example, if the spymaster gives the clue "fruit 2," their team might guess "apple" and "banana" because they are both fruits. If they guess correctly, the spymaster covers those cards with a colored agent card that matches their team's color. The objective of the game is to correctly guess all of the cards that match your team's color before the other team.

However, players must be careful not to guess cards belonging to the other team or the innocent bystanders, and definitely not the assassin card because doing so can cause your team to lose the game immediately.

Overall, Codenames is a fun and engaging word association game that is perfect for groups of all sizes!

- 1/4 teaspoon asafoetida
